blogPost-behover-mitt-foretag-en-cfo.title: Does my company need a CFO? 7 signs it's time
blogPost-behover-mitt-foretag-en-cfo.excerpt: Wondering whether your company needs a CFO? Read 7 clear signs that it's time — and why a modern CFO service can be smarter than a full-time hire.
blogPost-behover-mitt-foretag-en-cfo.seoTitle: Does my company need a CFO? 7 signs it's time
blogPost-behover-mitt-foretag-en-cfo.seoDescription: Wondering whether your company needs a CFO? Read 7 clear signs that it's time — and why a modern CFO service can be smarter than a full-time hire.

blocks.k1: You started the company because you're passionate about your product, your service or your idea. Not because you're passionate about year-end accounts, cash flow forecasts or tax planning.
blocks.k3: But somewhere along the way — maybe when revenue passed its first million, maybe when you hired your third employee — the financial questions started taking more and more of your time. Suddenly a bookkeeper who codes invoices after the fact is no longer enough. You need someone who looks ahead.
blocks.k5: The question most people then ask is: does my company need a CFO?
blocks.k7: The answer depends on where you are. In this article we go through 7 signs that it's time — and why the answer may not be a full-time CFO, but a more modern solution.
blocks.k9: What does a CFO actually do?
blocks.k11: Before we get into the signs, it's worth clarifying what a CFO actually does. It's easy to confuse the role with a finance assistant or an accounting consultant, but the difference is crucial.
blocks.k13: A finance assistant or bookkeeper handles what has already happened: bookkeeping, invoicing, ongoing accounting.
blocks.k15: An accounting consultant ensures the figures are correct and that you meet legal requirements: year-end accounts, tax returns, annual reports.
blocks.k17: A CFO looks ahead. The role is about:
blocks.k21: Identifying financial risks before they become problems
blocks.k23: Building decision support for investments, hiring and growth
blocks.k27: Ensuring the company's finances support — not slow down — the business plan
blocks.k29: In other words: the bookkeeper tells you where you've been. The CFO tells you where you're heading — and what you need to do to get there.
blocks.k31: 7 signs your company needs a CFO
blocks.k33: 1. You make financial decisions based on gut feeling
blocks.k35: You roughly know how things are going. Roughly how much money is in the account. Roughly what the margins are. But when you have to decide on a new hire, an investment in marketing or a move to larger premises, you lack figures to lean on.
blocks.k37: Why it's a sign: Decisions based on gut feeling work when the stakes are low. But the bigger the company gets, the more a wrong decision costs. A CFO gives you data-driven insights so every decision is based on reality, not assumptions.
blocks.k40: 2. You don't know exactly what your cash flow looks like in three months
blocks.k42: You can have high revenue and still end up in a liquidity crisis. It happens more often than you'd think — especially in growth phases where costs rise faster than revenue.
blocks.k44: Why it's a sign: Cash flow forecasts are one of the most important tools for avoiding financial surprises. If you don't have a clear picture of what cash flow looks like 30, 60 and 90 days ahead, you're missing a fundamental financial-control tool. A CFO builds and maintains that forecast for you.
blocks.k47: 3. You spend more than 5 hours a week on financial administration
blocks.k49: Time you spend chasing invoices, sorting out bank statements, reconciling the books or trying to understand your tax planning — that's time you're not spending building the company.
blocks.k51: Why it's a sign: As a founder or CEO, your time is the company's most expensive resource. If you spend more than 5 hours a week on financial administration you're paying a high price — not in money, but in growth that never happened. A CFO service frees up that time.
blocks.k54: 4. You have employees — but no salary optimization or workforce planning
blocks.k56: Hiring is one of the biggest costs for a growing company. But how do you set salaries? How do you plan for employer contributions, accrued holiday pay liability and pension costs? Have you calculated what the next hire actually costs — not just the gross salary, but the total cost?
blocks.k58: Why it's a sign: Personnel-related costs are often the largest item in an SME's budget. Without financial analysis you risk hiring too fast, setting salaries that squeeze margins, or missing opportunities to structure compensation more tax-efficiently.
blocks.k61: 5. You're preparing for a funding round or a bank loan
blocks.k63: Investors and banks want to see numbers. Not just historical results, but forecasts, key metrics, unit economics and a credible financial plan. They want to understand your burn rate, your runway and your path to profitability.
blocks.k65: Why it's a sign: Going into a funding round without financial documentation is like going into a salary negotiation without knowing your market value. A CFO prepares the financial material investors and banks expect — and presents it in a way that builds trust.
blocks.k68: 6. You've been surprised by a tax bill — at least once
blocks.k70: Suddenly there was VAT to pay that you hadn't counted on. Or the preliminary tax didn't match the actual result. Or you missed a tax-optimization opportunity that would have saved tens of thousands.
blocks.k72: Why it's a sign: Tax surprises are almost always a symptom of nobody looking ahead. A proactive CFO function ensures you have the right preliminary tax, plan for VAT and use the deductions and provisions available.
blocks.k75: 7. You know you're growing — but don't know if the growth is profitable
blocks.k77: Revenue is increasing. More customers, more projects, more employees. But what does the margin look like? Which customers are profitable? Which services or products contribute most to the result — and which eat it up?
blocks.k79: Why it's a sign: Growth without profitability control is one of the most common ways to build your way into a financial crisis. A CFO gives you real-time insight into which parts of the business create value — and which cost more than they return.
blocks.k82: Why a full-time CFO is rarely the answer for an SME
blocks.k84: If you recognized yourself in several of the signs above, it can be tempting to start looking for a CFO to hire. But for the vast majority of small and medium-sized companies, that isn't the right path.
blocks.k88: In Sweden, the salary for an experienced CFO is between SEK 70,000 and 120,000 per month — excluding employer contributions, pension and benefits. The total cost can end up at SEK 1.2–1.8 million per year.
blocks.k90: That's an investment that can be justified if you have revenue of SEK 50M+ and a complex business with several subsidiaries, international trade or regulatory requirements.
blocks.k92: But if you're a company with 5–30 employees and revenue of SEK 3–30M? Then you're paying for a resource you don't fully utilize. A CFO who works 40 hours a week simply isn't needed 40 hours a week in a company of that size.
blocks.k94: The modern alternative: a CFO function as a service
blocks.k96: This is where the concept of Finance-as-a-Service comes in. Instead of hiring a full-time CFO, you get access to the same expertise — but adapted to your company's actual needs.
blocks.k98: A modern CFO service gives you:
blocks.k100: Automated bookkeeping that reduces manual administration and the risk of errors
blocks.k102: Real-time cash flow forecasts that give you a clear picture of the finances ahead
blocks.k104: Proactive advisory that helps you make better decisions — not just report what already happened
blocks.k106: Data-driven insights that show exactly how each part of the business performs
blocks.k108: A complete finance solution that brings bookkeeping, advisory and reporting under one roof
blocks.k110: The advantage is simple: you pay for the financial expertise you actually need, without locking yourself into a full-time hire that costs more than it delivers.
blocks.k112: And unlike a traditional accounting firm — which focuses on the figures being correct after the fact — a modern CFO service is about helping you steer the company forward.
blocks.k114: What does it cost to not have a CFO?
blocks.k116: It's easy to think of CFO support as a cost. But the real cost is often not having it.
blocks.k120: A hire that costs SEK 15,000 more per month than necessary → SEK 180,000 per year
blocks.k122: A tax-deduction opportunity you missed → SEK 50,000–200,000
blocks.k124: A cash flow problem that forced you to take an expensive loan → tens of thousands in interest
blocks.k126: Decisions you postponed because you lacked data → impossible to quantify, but often the biggest cost
blocks.k128: Most business owners who get access to proactive financial control don't wonder if it was worth it. They wonder why they waited so long.
blocks.k130: Checklist: Is it time for a CFO function in your company?
blocks.k132: Answer the questions below. The more you answer yes to, the stronger the signal.
blocks.k134: You make financial decisions without a clear basis in numbers
blocks.k136: You lack a cash flow forecast for the next 90 days
blocks.k138: You spend more than 5 hours a week on financial administration
blocks.k140: You have employees but no analysis of total personnel costs
blocks.k142: You're planning to bring in external financing
blocks.k144: You've been surprised by tax payments at least once
blocks.k146: You know you're growing but are unsure whether it's profitable
blocks.k148: 0–2 yes: You'll probably manage with a good bookkeeper and accounting consultant — but keep your eyes open.
blocks.k150: 3–5 yes: It's becoming clear that you need proactive financial support. A CFO service can free up time and give you a better basis for decisions.
blocks.k152: 6–7 yes: You need a CFO function — and you probably needed it yesterday. The question isn't if, but how.
blocks.k156: Needing a CFO isn't about the company's size. It's about the company's complexity and where it's heading.
blocks.k158: If you make financial decisions without a clear basis, if cash flow is a black box and if you spend hours every week on administration instead of on your core business — then it's time.
blocks.k160: But the solution doesn't have to be a full-time hire. With a modern CFO service you get access to the expertise and tools you need, adapted to your company's actual situation and budget.
blocks.k162: Financial support should free up time, not take it.
blocks.k164: Common questions about CFO services for small companies
blocks.k166: What does an external CFO service cost?
blocks.k168: The cost varies depending on the company's size, complexity and which services are included. An external CFO service or Finance-as-a-Service solution can cost anywhere from SEK 5,000 to 30,000 per month — a fraction of what a full-time CFO costs. Many providers offer scalable pricing that grows with your company.
blocks.k170: What's the difference between an accounting consultant and a CFO?
blocks.k172: An accounting consultant ensures the bookkeeping is correct and that laws and regulations are followed — the focus is on what has already happened. A CFO looks ahead: cash flow forecasts, decision support, tax optimization, financial strategy. You need both — but they don't replace each other.
blocks.k174: Can a company with 5 employees really need a CFO?
blocks.k176: Yes. It's not about the number of employees but about how complex your finances are and what decisions you face. A consulting company with 5 employees that's growing fast, handles project accounting and plans to bring in investors has completely different financial needs than a pure bookkeeping service can meet.
blocks.k180: Finance-as-a-Service means you get access to a complete finance function — bookkeeping, reporting, cash flow forecasts and proactive advisory — as a service instead of building it in-house. It combines technology and expertise to give you the same quality as a large company's finance department, but at a cost that fits an SME.
blocks.k182: How do I know whether I need a bookkeeper, an accounting consultant or a CFO?
blocks.k184: If you need help with ongoing bookkeeping and invoicing, a bookkeeper is enough. If you need year-end accounts, tax returns and compliance, you need an accounting consultant. If you need cash flow forecasts, decision support for growth and proactive financial advisory, you need a CFO function. Many modern finance services combine all three under one roof.
blocks.k186: This article is written by the MinCFO editorial team and is based on experience from Swedish small and medium-sized companies. The article does not constitute financial advice — contact a financial advisor if you need guidance in your specific situation.

blogPost-ekonomiska-misstag-foretag.excerpt: Are you making these common financial mistakes? Learn what small companies often get wrong — and how to avoid it before it costs you money.
blogPost-ekonomiska-misstag-foretag.seoTitle: 5 financial mistakes that cost small business owners thousands every month
blogPost-ekonomiska-misstag-foretag.seoDescription: Are you making these common financial mistakes? Learn what small companies often get wrong — and how to avoid it before it costs you money.

blocks.k1: Running a company is about making decisions. Every day. Some feel small. Others big. But many of the most important decisions have one thing in common: they affect your finances.
blocks.k3: And here a problem arises. Financial mistakes rarely show up immediately. They build up over time — often quietly — until they suddenly have consequences. It could be:
blocks.k5: The cash flow that doesn't last
blocks.k11: And in hindsight it's easy to see what went wrong. But considerably harder to spot in time. In this article we go through 5 of the most common financial mistakes small companies make — and what you can do to avoid them.
blocks.k13: Mistake 1: You don't have a grip on your cash flow
blocks.k15: This is the most common — and most critical — mistake. Many companies focus on the result. Revenue. Profit. Growth. But it's not the result that determines whether you make it. It's cash flow.
blocks.k17: You can be profitable on paper — and still run out of money. It happens more often than you'd think. Especially in companies that are growing.
blocks.k23: Costs arise before revenue comes in
blocks.k29: You end up in a situation where:
blocks.k31: The money in the account isn't enough
blocks.k35: You have to take a loan or slow down the business

blogPost-kassaflodesprognos-smaforetag.title: Cash flow forecast for small businesses – how to get control over liquidity
blogPost-kassaflodesprognos-smaforetag.excerpt: Learn how to create a cash flow forecast that protects your company from liquidity crises. A practical guide with common mistakes and concrete steps for Swedish SMEs.
blogPost-kassaflodesprognos-smaforetag.seoTitle: Cash flow forecast for small businesses – how to get control over liquidity
blogPost-kassaflodesprognos-smaforetag.seoDescription: Learn how to create a cash flow forecast that protects your company from liquidity crises. A practical guide with common mistakes and concrete steps for Swedish SMEs.

blocks.k1: There are companies that go bankrupt even though they're profitable.
blocks.k3: It sounds paradoxical, but it happens more often than most people think. According to UC, thousands of Swedish companies become insolvent every year — not because they lack customers or revenue, but because the money runs out at the wrong time.
blocks.k5: The cause is almost always the same: insufficient cash flow control.
blocks.k7: A cash flow forecast is the tool that prevents this. Yet the majority of Swedish small businesses don't have a working one. In this guide we go through what a cash flow forecast is, why it's business-critical, and how to build one that actually works in practice.
blocks.k9: What is a cash flow forecast?
blocks.k11: A cash flow forecast is a forward-looking calculation of how much money is expected to come into and go out of your company over a given period — usually 30, 60 or 90 days.
blocks.k13: Unlike an income statement, which shows whether you're profitable over time, the cash flow forecast shows whether you have money in the account right now and in the near term.
blocks.k17: Perspective — The income statement is backward-looking, the cash flow forecast is forward-looking.
blocks.k20: Measures — The income statement measures profitability, the cash flow forecast measures liquidity.
blocks.k23: The question it answers — Income statement: “Are we making money?” Cash flow forecast: “Do we have money?”
blocks.k26: Time horizon — Income statement quarterly or annually. Cash flow forecast weekly or monthly.
blocks.k29: Warning of problems — The income statement warns after the fact. The cash flow forecast warns in advance.
blocks.k32: You can have an income statement showing profit and still be left with no money in the account. This happens, for example, when:
blocks.k34: Customers pay late (30–90 day payment terms)
blocks.k36: You have large outgoing payments such as salaries, VAT or tax concentrated at a few points in time
blocks.k38: You invest in growth (inventory, hiring, marketing) before revenue has time to catch up
blocks.k40: Why does your company in particular need a cash flow forecast?
blocks.k42: You avoid liquidity crises before they arise
blocks.k44: The biggest benefit of a cash flow forecast is that it gives you time to act. If you see that the account will be empty in six weeks, you have six weeks to solve it — by postponing an investment, negotiating payment terms or securing a credit facility.
blocks.k46: Without the forecast you discover the problem the day the invoice is due.
blocks.k50: “Can we afford to hire now?” “Can we invest in new equipment?” “Should we take on this project?”
blocks.k52: Every such decision requires the same basis: do you know what cash flow looks like over the coming months? With a cash flow forecast you can answer these questions with figures instead of gut feeling.
blocks.k54: You strengthen your position with banks and investors
blocks.k56: If you need financing — whether it's a bank loan, an overdraft facility or a funding round — the cash flow forecast is one of the first documents requested. It shows that you understand your company's financial dynamics and that you plan proactively.
blocks.k58: A business owner who can show a clear liquidity forecast signals control. That builds trust.
blocks.k60: You spot patterns you'd otherwise miss
blocks.k62: Cash flow in a typical Swedish SME rarely follows an even curve. There are peaks and troughs — often linked to:
blocks.k64: VAT periods (quarterly or monthly depending on revenue)
blocks.k72: Without a forecast you only see the current account balance. With a forecast you see the patterns — and can plan around them.
blocks.k74: How to build a cash flow forecast in 5 steps
blocks.k76: Step 1: Map all expected incoming payments
blocks.k78: Start with the revenue side. List all expected incoming payments over the next 90 days:
blocks.k80: Invoiced revenue — what have you invoiced and when is payment expected? Count on the actual payment pattern, not the due date. If your average customer pays 5 days after the due date, adjust the forecast accordingly.
blocks.k82: Recurring revenue — subscriptions, contracts with fixed monthly amounts, retainers.
blocks.k84: Expected new sales — be conservative. Don't count on deals that aren't signed.
blocks.k86: Other incoming payments — tax refunds, grants, dividends from subsidiaries.
blocks.k88: Common mistake: Counting on revenue that is “almost certain” but not yet confirmed. In a cash flow forecast there is only money that is invoiced or contracted. Everything else belongs in an optimistic scenario — not the base plan.
blocks.k91: Step 2: List all expected outgoing payments
blocks.k93: Now the other side. Go through all costs and outgoing payments:
blocks.k97: Salaries and employer social security contributions
blocks.k119: VAT (monthly or quarterly, depending on revenue)
blocks.k129: Common mistake: Forgetting the periodic costs. The VAT payment in April, the holiday pay disbursements in June and the annual insurance premium in January create big troughs in cash flow if they aren't planned in.
blocks.k132: Step 3: Calculate net cash flow per week or month
blocks.k134: For each period (week or month, depending on how detailed you want to be):
blocks.k136: Net cash flow = Incoming payments − Outgoing payments
blocks.k140: Closing balance = Opening balance + Net cash flow
blocks.k142: A simplified monthly view can look like this:
blocks.k144: April: opening SEK 320,000 · in 480,000 · out 410,000 · net +70,000 → closing SEK 390,000.
blocks.k147: May: opening SEK 390,000 · in 440,000 · out 520,000 · net −80,000 → closing SEK 310,000.
blocks.k150: June: opening SEK 310,000 · in 390,000 · out 560,000 · net −170,000 → closing SEK 140,000.
blocks.k153: July: opening SEK 140,000 · in 350,000 · out 380,000 · net −30,000 → closing SEK 110,000.
blocks.k156: In the example above we see that cash flow gradually weakens over the summer — a common pattern for service companies. Without the forecast, the liquidity pressure in July would have come as a surprise. With the forecast you can act as early as April.
blocks.k160: Look at the forecast and mark periods where:
blocks.k162: The closing balance approaches zero — or falls below the level you need to feel secure (a good rule of thumb: at least 2 months of fixed costs in reserve)
blocks.k164: Net cash flow is negative several months in a row — that's a pattern that requires action, not just luck
blocks.k166: Large outgoing payments coincide — VAT, salaries and a quarterly insurance premium in the same week can create a temporary crisis even in an otherwise healthy company
blocks.k170: A cash flow forecast isn't just an analysis tool — it's a decision tool. When you identify a critical period, plan concrete actions:
blocks.k172: Customers pay too late — Introduce shorter payment terms, send reminders proactively, offer a discount for fast payment.
blocks.k175: Large payments bunched together — Negotiate payment plans, spread costs over several months.
blocks.k178: Seasonal dip in revenue — Build up a cash reserve during strong months, plan marketing efforts ahead of the weak period.
blocks.k181: Fast growth strains the cash — Secure a credit facility in advance, adapt the investment pace to cash flow.
blocks.k184: 5 common mistakes that ruin the cash flow forecast
blocks.k188: A forecast made in January and never updated is useless in March. The cash flow forecast must be a living document updated at least every two weeks — preferably every week.
blocks.k190: 2. You're too optimistic about incoming payments
blocks.k192: It's human to count on the best-case scenario. But in cash flow planning that's dangerous. Base it on the probable scenario and have a pessimistic scenario ready.
blocks.k196: VAT is the most common cause of unexpected cash flow troughs in Swedish small businesses. If you report VAT quarterly, the payment can be hundreds of thousands of SEK — and if it's not in the forecast it creates a crisis out of nothing.
blocks.k198: 4. You confuse revenue and incoming payments
blocks.k200: The fact that you've invoiced SEK 500,000 in March doesn't mean you have SEK 500,000 available. If the payment term is 30 days and the customer pays 10 days late, you have the money in May. Your forecast must be based on when the money actually arrives in the account, not when the invoice is sent.
blocks.k204: A forecast so complex that no one bothers to update it is worse than a simple forecast that's actually used. Start simple — you can always refine it later.
blocks.k206: When Excel is no longer enough
blocks.k208: Many business owners start with a spreadsheet. It works — for a while. But Excel-based cash flow forecasts have clear limitations:
blocks.k210: Manual entry — every figure has to be updated by hand, which takes time and increases the risk of errors
blocks.k212: No connection to actual transactions — the forecast lives in its own world, separate from the bookkeeping
blocks.k214: No automatic updating — invoices that get paid, costs that arise or contracts that change aren't updated automatically
blocks.k216: Hard to share — if more people on the team need to see the forecast, version control quickly becomes a problem
blocks.k218: Modern finance services solve this by connecting the cash flow forecast directly to the accounting system. Incoming and outgoing payments are updated in real time, invoices that fall due appear automatically, and the forecast is adjusted continuously without manual work.
blocks.k220: The result is a forecast that's always accurate — not one that was accurate the day it was created.
blocks.k222: A cash flow forecast in practice: an example
blocks.k226: Company: A consulting firm in Gothenburg with 8 employees and SEK 6 million in annual revenue.
blocks.k229: The situation: The company has had a strong spring with several new customers. The owner is considering hiring another consultant after the summer.
blocks.k232: Without a cash flow forecast: The owner looks at the account balance (SEK 580,000), sees that it looks good, and decides to go ahead with the recruitment.
blocks.k235: With a cash flow forecast: The forecast shows that:
blocks.k238: Three large customers have 45-day payment terms, which creates a delay in incoming payments
blocks.k240: The VAT payment in August (Q2 VAT) is SEK 190,000
blocks.k242: The holiday pay disbursements in June–July take a further SEK 240,000
blocks.k244: Revenue decreases during the holiday period while fixed costs remain
blocks.k246: The forecast shows that the closing balance at the end of August lands at SEK 85,000 — far below the level required to safely hire in September.
blocks.k248: Decision with the forecast: Postpone the recruitment to October. Or: renegotiate the payment terms with the three large customers. Or: secure an overdraft facility as a buffer.
blocks.k251: The same decision. Completely different outcomes depending on whether you have the basis or not.
blocks.k253: Checklist: Get started with your cash flow forecast
blocks.k255: Gather all invoiced but unpaid customer receivables and their expected payment dates
blocks.k257: List all fixed costs per month (salaries, rent, licenses, loans)
blocks.k259: Map periodic costs over the next 12 months (VAT, tax, annual fees)
blocks.k261: Calculate the average payment time from customers (not terms — actual behavior)
blocks.k263: Build your first 90-day forecast with opening balance, incoming and outgoing payments per month
blocks.k265: Identify periods with negative net cash flow and create action plans
blocks.k267: Set a routine: update the forecast every week or every two weeks
blocks.k269: Consider automating by connecting the forecast to your accounting system
blocks.k273: A cash flow forecast isn't an advanced finance tool for large corporations. It's a fundamental control tool for every company that wants to grow without risking running out of money.
blocks.k275: Most liquidity crises in Swedish small businesses could have been prevented with a simple forward-looking forecast and 15 minutes of work per week.
blocks.k277: Start simple. Update regularly. And above all: use the forecast as a basis for decisions, not just as a report to look at.
blocks.k279: Your company's finances should give you control — not sleepless nights.
blocks.k281: Common questions about cash flow forecasts
blocks.k283: How far ahead should a cash flow forecast extend?
blocks.k285: For most small businesses, 90 days (3 months) is a good horizon. It provides enough foresight to act on problems without the forecast becoming too uncertain. Companies with longer sales cycles or large seasonal variations may need a 6–12 month forecast, but with less detail the further out in time.
blocks.k287: What's the difference between a cash flow forecast and a liquidity budget?
blocks.k289: A liquidity budget is the planned version — what you expect cash flow to be based on budget and plans. A cash flow forecast is updated continuously with actual figures and adjusted assumptions. In practice you want both: the budget as the target picture and the forecast as the reality check.
blocks.k291: How often should I update the cash flow forecast?
blocks.k293: At least every two weeks, preferably every week. If your company moves fast — many invoices, rapid changes, tight margins — it may be justified to update daily. With an automated solution connected to the accounting system the forecast updates in real time.
blocks.k295: Can I make a cash flow forecast in Excel?
blocks.k297: Yes, absolutely — and it's a good place to start. But Excel requires manual updating, has no connection to your actual transactions and makes it hard to keep the forecast current. Most companies that start in Excel eventually move to an automated solution.
blocks.k299: What do I do if the cash flow forecast shows that the money isn't enough?
blocks.k301: That's exactly the purpose of the forecast — to give you time to act. Depending on the situation you can: renegotiate payment terms with customers, postpone planned investments, apply for an overdraft facility, negotiate installment payments with suppliers, or intensify sales efforts. The earlier you see the problem, the more options you have.
